info.bio: Pocos artistas han dejado un impacto tan profundo en la música contemporánea como Emmylou Harris. Bendecida con una voz cristalina, un incansable espíritu creativo y un gran talento musical, su trayectoria ha marcado una senda singular, llevando con orgullo la antorcha de la música Americana, recogiendo así el relevo de su mentor, Gram Parsons. Con la única excepción de Neil Young, ninguna otra estrella ha establecido una obra musical tan consistentemente iconoclasta, ecléctica o atrevida.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …albums, G.P. (1972) and especially Grievous Angel (1973), that consolidated the legend of a "poet maudit" who lived fast and died young (in 1973). Emmylou Harris (1), the angelic soprano who accompanied Gram Parsons' urban nightmares, belonged to a new batch of country-pop singers (Linda Ronstadt, Maria Muldaur, Kim Carnes) who bridged the world of Nashville and the world of rock music. Harris was typical of the way these female singers were appropriating the rock repertory, although her best work would come much later in her career,…

podcast.title: Meeting Linda Ronstadt (1973)
podcast.body: Emmylou Harris met Linda Ronstadt at a loud, rowdy honky-tonk called the Liberty Bar in Houston in 1973. Ronstadt was so impressed by Harris's singing that the atmosphere in the bar would quiet when she performed, leading Ronstadt to decide to become her friend and musical collaborator. "Linda Ronstadt and Emileu met at this honky-tonk in Houston called the Liberty Bar in 1973 and the way Linda describes it it was this loud, rowdy place which would get really quiet when Emileu sang because she is just that good."

podcast.title: Quote on Reinvention and Authenticity (2006)
podcast.body: In 2006, Emmylou Harris articulated that each generation must "reinvent itself poetically and probably music," finding its own authenticity by absorbing old music and "spinning it out ourselves," thereby adding something from one's own experience. "every generation has to reinvent itself poetically and probably music but we have to find our own authenticity absorbing the old music and spinning it out ourselves that's an authentic way of reinventing oneself because you're going to add something to it that's coming from your own experience."

podcast.title: Collaboration Attempt with Dolly Parton and Linda Ronstadt (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: Following an impressive performance on Dolly Parton's TV show with Dolly and Linda Ronstadt, the trio attempted to record an album together shortly after. However, it "didn't sound right" and faced contractual issues, delaying their successful "Trio" album until 1987. "No Dolly and Emmy Lou and Linda were as impressed as anyone with how they sounded and tried to make a record not long after that. It didn't sound right and I think there were some contractual issues."

podcast.title: Collaboration with Gram Parsons
podcast.body: Emmylou Harris worked very closely with Gram Parsons, whose band The Flying Burrito Brothers was instrumental in setting the stage for the country rock style popular in the 1970s, influencing groups like the early Eagles. "She worked really closely with Graham Parsons whose flying burrito brothers band really set the stage for the country rock style that was so popular in the 70s you know think early Eagles."

podcast.title: Early Folk Career and Discovery
podcast.body: Emmylou Harris began her career as a folk singer in 1969. She was discovered by Chris Hillman at a club outside Washington, D.C., which led to Hillman suggesting her to Gram Parsons for his solo album, ultimately sparking their iconic collaboration. "Now she started out as a folk singer in 1969. Chris Hillman heard her sing at a club outside of Washington, D.C."

podcast.title: Grief Over Gram Parsons' Death
podcast.body: Harris was profoundly distraught by Gram Parsons' death, having believed she would sing with him for the rest of her life. She channeled her feelings of loss and grief into the song "Boulder to Birmingham," which became a very important outlet for her. "She thought that she would be singing with Graham for the rest of her life."

podcast.title: Living Gram Parsons' Vision
podcast.body: Emmylou Harris is seen as embodying Gram Parsons' vision of "cosmic American music" through her ability to authentically sing across multiple genres like gospel, bluegrass, country, and country rock. She describes her approach as "bleeding outside the lines sometimes," delivering diverse music with one of the most beautiful voices. "In this way, I think she is living out Graham's vision of cosmic American music, a little of this, a little of that, all with one of the most beautiful voices that you have ever heard."

podcast.title: Loss of Musical Companions
podcast.body: Even years later, Harris finds it hard to accept the loss of many beloved musicians she admired and sang with, including Waylon Jennings and Townes Van Zandt, highlighting the deep personal and professional connections she forged. "Even now, she has said it is hard to believe for her that so many of the people that were in her life and that she loved to hear sing and sing with wail and Jennings and towns van Zant just to name a couple that they're gone."

podcast.title: Quote on Country Music
podcast.body: Harris used a vivid metaphor to describe her relationship with country music: "I smoked, but I didn't inhale." This implies a nuanced engagement with the genre, appreciating its essence without fully succumbing to all its traditional constraints. "I smoked, but I didn't inhale."

podcast.title: Strong Emotional Connection with Parsons
podcast.body: While it was questioned whether Emmylou Harris and Gram Parsons had a physical relationship (Parsons was married, Harris was divorced with a child), they shared a very strong emotional, and possibly spiritual, connection. This deep bond fueled their intense musical chemistry. "There are many who questioned whether or not Emileu and Graham had a physical relationship too, but Graham was married. Emileu was divorced with a child, and they just had a very strong emotional and maybe also a spiritual connection."

podcast.title: Unprepared for a Life Without Parsons
podcast.body: At the age of 23-25, Emmylou Harris was emotionally unprepared for a career and life without Gram Parsons, reflecting the profound impact of his death on her personal and professional path. "I think a young Emileu was just not prepared for a career or a life without Graham."
